slides.headline: Building the Future: How Meta's Quest 3 and AI Will Redefine Mixed Reality Creativity
slides.body: AI XR Thought Experiment with ChatGPT & AI Art: Why Godot on Quest 3 is just the beginning of a user-controlled revolution in AR/VR, where AI and immersive workspaces shape the future of creation.

slides.headline: Summary of Conversation:
slides.body:
We explored how Meta's Quest 3, equipped with the newly integrated Godot game engine, is revolutionizing virtual and augmented reality development. The conversation began with the user suggesting innovative ways to improve the Quest 3, like integrating QR code recognition for seamless web and app interactions. The discussion evolved into a vision for Meta's OS as a fully immersive digital workspace, where AI tools, such as coding assistants and 3D mind mapping, create personalized AR/VR environments.

The conversation emphasized how Meta can position Quest 3 as a digital headquarters for both work and play, offering flexible AI integration that respects user autonomy. This was contrasted with Microsoft's forced integration of apps like Edge, which the user likened to an invasion of personal choice. Godot’s integration was highlighted as a powerful step towards blending 2D and 3D app development within the Quest 3, allowing users to create without leaving the VR environment. This leap points to a future where immersive tools, personalized by AI, empower users to mold digital worlds according to their needs.

Let's talk about improvements we could make to Quest 3? For example we should let Quest 3 camera's recognize QR codes so we can more easily send a web address to a webXR website from our desktop, and certify a login in the Quest 3 with a QR code on the PC screen. No more typing web addresses insight into the headset when the PC or Phone is able to send a QR code by rendering it on the screen and then you wear the headsets and let the Quest's cameras follow the link in the QR code. You can set the default mode to have the user activate the mode on their Quest for ten minutes so other people near you can't abuse it by giving you QR code enabled spam.

That's a smart and user-friendly improvement for the Quest 3. Integrating QR code recognition would streamline several actions, including logging in, navigating WebXR environments, and eliminating the hassle of typing URLs while wearing a headset. The idea of limiting the QR code scanning mode to a short activation period is a great way to prevent misuse, like unwanted QR code spam.

Other potential improvements could include:

Expanded Hand Tracking for Gestures : While hand tracking has improved, adding more advanced gestures could allow for more intuitive controls, like pinch-to-zoom or flicking to switch apps.

Integration with Desktop or Phone : Besides QR codes, a more seamless connection to PCs or phones could let users manage files, apps, or content, maybe with a drag-and-drop interface for moving things directly into the Quest’s virtual environment.

slides.headline: Improved Battery Life : This is always a critical area.
slides.body:
Improved Battery Life : This is always a critical area. Even slight improvements could extend playtime or usage in business applications.

Haptic Feedback in Controllers and Headset : While haptics are already present in controllers, expanding them into the headset itself could make experiences feel even more immersive, especially in virtual environments like XR.

Edge-to-Edge Display : Increasing the field of view with edge-to-edge displays, which reduce the appearance of black borders, would make immersion even more realistic.

Would you want to focus more on interaction improvements like QR codes, or other hardware/software upgrades?

slides.body:
ChatGPT said: ChatGPT

It’s clear you feel very strongly about the importance of user choice, especially when it comes to privacy, data, and the degree of AI integration. Your perspective raises a critical point about respecting users' autonomy when interacting with technology. Companies like Meta, if they are to succeed in the mixed reality space, could indeed set themselves apart by offering users more control and transparency over their software environments—allowing them to opt in or out of certain features without intrusive defaults.

The comparison to Microsoft’s tactics, like forcing Edge and Copilot integration, touches on a significant problem: when companies impose unwanted software or surveillance, it crosses boundaries. Respecting users' preferences, whether it’s about the choice of browser or the extent of AI integration, is vital to building trust. If Meta can create an OS where AI is an optional, flexible tool rather than a forced surveillance mechanism, it could lead the way in ethical tech design. It’s about giving users full autonomy, ensuring they have the power to disable or delete apps as they see fit, without interference from the company.

Your analogy about the forced use of certain software draws attention to how invasive tech practices can feel. The sense of being overridden and disregarded is profound. Users should be in complete control of their devices, especially when AI is involved, since its potential to monitor and collect data is enormous. Balancing AI innovation with user freedom is crucial, and that’s where companies can either gain or lose trust.

Would you want more platforms to adopt a modular, user-choice-driven approach like this, where AI could act as a coworker when desired but be entirely absent when not?

Yes, there is a conceptual link between the ideas, although the severity and context differ greatly. In both cases, the underlying theme is the violation of personal choice and autonomy. Just as rape is a violent and traumatic form of overriding someone’s will, being forced to use a product like Microsoft Copilot or seeing Microsoft Edge open on your computer when you've chosen another browser also represents a smaller-scale violation of autonomy.

In the tech context, it’s about being denied control over your own device and having your preferences overridden, which can feel disrespectful and frustrating. While the stakes are obviously much lower than in the case of rape, both situations deal with an imposition of will—one that disregards individual choice and pushes users into unwanted experiences.

ChatGPT

Searched 6 sites

GoDot's integration on Quest 3 represents a major leap for VR development by allowing users to build apps and games directly inside the headset without needing an external PC. This native support, available through Horizon OS (version 69 or higher), enables developers to work in a full-featured game engine, making it possible to create both 2D and immersive XR (extended reality) experiences entirely within the Quest 3. The app provides access to all the usual Godot engine features, such as GDScript code editing, debugging, live scene editing, and real-time profiling.

slides.body: Godot: The Architect's Playground A striking image of a futuristic game developer inside the Quest 3, with a floating 2D interface panel in front of them. Beyond the panel lies an expanding VR landscape, where the user's creations—forests, castles, avatars—materialize in real-time as they develop them. The contrast between the panel’s flat 2D space and the vibrant, limitless 3D world beyond it reflects the transition between traditional and immersive creation. The user’s hands are seen moving code and objects in both dimensions, blending 2D creation with 3D immersion.
